text: The following question stood in the name of  Ms Mariam Jaafar –   2 To ask the Minister for Health (a) whether insurers offering massive additional coverage for cancer treatment through their riders is a cause for concern for the Ministry; and (b) whether such riders undermine efforts to contain cancer drug costs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: My response will also cover the matters raised in the questions by Mr Louis Chua1 and Mr Saktiandi Supaat2 which are scheduled for a subsequent Sitting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I would invite Members to seek clarifications, if need be.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If their questions have been addressed, it may not be necessary for them to proceed with the questions for future Sittings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Eighty-four percent received treatment in Public Healthcare Institutions, or PHIs, and 16% in private medical institutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This proportion has remained stable over the past few years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is sufficient to cover the essential cancer drug services incurred by more than nine in 10 subsidised patients in our PHIs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Other Members raised concerns that generous insurance coverage, especially Integrated Shield Plans, or IPs, and IP plus riders provided by commercial insurance companies, will continue to contribute to the rapid escalation of cancer drug prices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But first let me explain the key reasons for the rapid rise in cancer drug prices over the past years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With the Cancer Drug List, or CDL, announced in August 2021, drug companies have lowered their prices in order to include their drugs in the CDL so that they can get financing coverage, namely subsidy, plus MediShield, MediShield, MediShield Life and IP coverage.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Since these changes, we have negotiated an average cost reduction of 30% for most drugs, and over 60% for some drugs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We can plough the money saved on procurement costs into more subsidies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Overseas studies have found that about half of new cancer treatments were introduced without evidence of benefit to survival or quality of life.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, patients and their loved ones all hope for a cure. "As-charged" insurance policies, including IPs and riders, are policies where coverage can be effectively limitless and patients have limited co-payment; they further encourage this practice where non-cost-effective cancer treatments are prescribed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It sends a strong signal to patients and doctors to use clinically proven and cost-effective treatments, which are covered by subsidies and MediShield Life from 1 September 2022 and IPs from April 2023.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are riders which can still cover non-CDL treatments, but with the policy changes effected by the CDL, the costs of these treatments will have to be reflected in the rider premiums, rather than loaded onto MediShield Life and IP premiums for the broad majority.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In other words, the high cost of non-cost-effective drugs will not be socialised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Thirdly, the mark-up of cancer drugs by some healthcare providers may be quite significant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is, again, encouraged by "as-charged" IPs and riders, which provided for effectively limitless claims.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH had, in 2018, taken steps to moderate this by requiring all new riders to have a minimum co-payment of 5% and typically capped at $3,000 a year, for treatments from panel doctors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For cancer drug treatments, most IPs provide coverage of up to five times that of the MediShield Life limit for treatments on the CDL.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is sufficient to cover cost-effective CDL treatments at up to 2.5 times that of unsubsidised PHI prices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A few Members have also raised concerns that the new CDL limits for riders – such as 18 times of the MediShield Life claim limits – continue to be high and can push up cancer drug prices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will review how to improve the transparency of cancer drug prices to help patients make informed decisions and encourage providers to calibrate their mark-ups.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are also monitoring cancer drug claims and coverage closely and will work with the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to take further steps to regulate IPs and riders if costs continue to escalate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the meantime, we urge individuals to consider the long-term cost of the insurance products they purchase against the level of protection they need.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The fact is that our CDL is more extensive than similar listings in most developed countries, including South Korea, Australia and the United Kingdom.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS also requires insurance intermediaries to properly assess if a health insurance product is suitable for a customer's needs and financial situation before recommending the product to the customer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, would the Ministry be prepared to work with the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCCS) to develop a platform like Price Kaki, which will allow patients to compare cancer drug prices across the public, as well as the private hospitals and clinics?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, pharmaceutical companies may be selling the same medications to Singaporeans at higher prices than other countries with comparable economic situations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry be prepared to work with MTI and CCCS to investigate this?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think MOH can work on this together with the Singapore Medical Council and the medical community, without involving the CCCS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Such price transparency itself will be quite useful.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is something that we will study and I had mentioned that in my reply.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the Member's second question, differential pricing across countries, this is widely practised by many global suppliers, including by pharmaceutical companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should first say that pharmaceutical companies are our close partners in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, they are the ones who provided us with vaccines and a way out of the COVID-19 pandemic crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we also understand that they incur quite a lot of research costs which have to be recovered through drug costs when something is approved and able to be distributed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In so doing, they too, maximise their revenue by pricing the drugs in different markets differently.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you do so, it crosses our cost-effectiveness threshold, it can be in the CDL, and therefore, it can be subsidised and enjoy MediShield Life claims." So far, we have been quite successful.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should reiterate a point raised in my former reply just now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, our CDL is actually quite extensive and, in fact, longer and more comprehensive than many similar listings in many developed countries around the world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand that the CDL is a positive development for our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But at the same time, a lot of the insurers are responding very quickly to this legislation and introducing various riders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand from the Minister's response that the Ministry is looking into this.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, my question is whether the Ministry will look into whether insurance companies are profiteering from this.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And eventually, the concern is whether or not this could all end up as higher premiums for the various policyholders as a result.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Before I directly answer the question, let me explain what is happening now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the past, as we know, MediShield Life provides the basic level of protection.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Above that, there is IP; and above whatever IP does not provide, riders would provide.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, you look at the cake as three layers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the past, what happens is, an IP has limitless claims.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it requires some co-payment and riders to sit on top of IPs to cover part of the co-payment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But with the recent changes, that relationship has been flipped.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because an IP now has quite a strict coverage of four, five times of MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, IP has lower coverage; it also does not cover so many drugs because non-CDL drugs are no longer covered; IP coverage has shrunk.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But now, the ballon is squeezed out into the rider space.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Insurance companies now come in with riders with 18 times coverage – so, not "as-charged" but 18 times or a very high absolute number.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think there is an impact now where it is no longer "as-charged" but the entire IP plus rider is now capped, albeit a very high cap.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The way consumers respond will be quite key.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If consumers heed our advice, that if you just look at our CDL which is quite comprehensive and that IP coverage is actually quite adequate; and if they stick to just buying IP, then I think the problem can be addressed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When it comes to the riders, they should look at the price.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Riders have to price in higher coverage plus more drug coverage, so they will be priced higher; and you cannot use MediSave – you can only use cash.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if rider demand goes down and most people think IP is enough for them, I think we have addressed the problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if consumer behaviour does not change and consumers continue to buy riders, notwithstanding high premiums, then, I think I agree with the Member, we may have a problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am not sure I would describe the insurance sector that way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am not sure they are profiteering from it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But because they compete, they try to fight for market share, they offer a wide coverage – sometimes, it is, in the long term, not very sustainable for their business.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In healthcare, it is a very complex system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Regular market economics do not quite work and if need be, if we have to regulate, we will do so.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, can I ask the Minister one supplementary question: will the payout, the claims on the rider, affect the MediShield Life greatly?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the rider itself is an outlet; and we can cover more drugs and higher limits, and it should be priced accordingly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: My sense is that based on today's design, the answer is "no".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the past, the answer is "yes", and it is not fair to the great majority who do not use non-cost-effective drugs.
